lead: OBD-II, short for On-Board Diagnostics second generation, is a standard that lets one scan tool plug into almost any car made after the late 1990s and read emissions-related faults. It fixes the 16-pin connector, the electrical pins, the message services and the fault-code format. A mechanic, a fleet owner or an inspection centre uses it to find why the malfunction indicator lamp is on, to read live sensor data, and to check that the engine control unit has finished its self-tests. The same socket also gives the vehicle identification number.
prereq: You need: Chapter 6.2 for CAN frames, identifiers and the physical layer, because most OBD-II messages travel on CAN.

blocks.text: OBD-II began as an emissions rule. Before it, each maker had its own connector and its own codes, so a workshop needed many adapters. The standard, often called J1962 for the connector, makes the socket shape and pin functions common. The socket sits under the dashboard near the steering column, within reach of the driver. Pins 4 and 5 are chassis and signal ground. Pin 16 is battery positive, usually through a fuse. Pins 6 and 14 are CAN high and CAN low. Pins 7 and 15 are the older K-line and L-line pair. Pins 2 and 10 carry the older J1850 bus. Other pins are left for manufacturer use or left blank.

The scan tool powers up from pin 16 and pin 4 or 5. It then listens on the bus pins. A tool that finds no reply on pins 6 and 14 can try the older pins. This fallback lets one tool serve cars from different bus generations.

A scan tool sends a request service, and an ECU replies. A service is a one-byte command number inside a diagnostic message. Service 01 reads current data. Service 02 reads the freeze frame, a snapshot of data stored when a fault was set. Service 03 reads stored diagnostic trouble codes (DTCs). Service 04 clears codes. Service 05 reads oxygen sensor test results. Service 06 reads on-board test results. Service 09 reads the vehicle identification number (VIN). Service 0A reads permanent codes. A parameter identifier (PID) names one measured value. A reply to service 01 has service 0x41, then the PID, then data bytes A, B and so on.

blocks.where: RPM is engine speed in revolutions per minute; A is the first data byte (0 to 255); B is the second data byte (0 to 255); 256 combines the two bytes into a 16-bit raw count; 4 converts the raw count to rpm because one count is 0.25 rpm.

blocks.text: PID 0C is engine speed. Many PIDs use one data byte, some use two, and a few use four. The scan tool must apply the scaling for that PID; the raw bytes alone are not the physical value. PID 0D, vehicle speed, uses one byte A in km/h. PID 05, coolant temperature, uses one byte A and the formula A − 40 in °C.

sections.h3: Fault codes, monitors and the lamp

blocks.text: A DTC has one letter, then four hexadecimal digits. Hexadecimal means base-16 digits 0-9 and A-F. The letter gives the system: P is powertrain, C is chassis, B is body, and U is network. In P0301, P means powertrain, the first digit 0 means a generic code defined by the standard, the second digit 3 means ignition system or misfire, and 01 means cylinder 1. A first digit 1 would mean a manufacturer-specific code. P0301 is a generic misfire code for cylinder 1.

Readiness monitors are self-tests inside the ECU, such as catalyst, oxygen sensor, evaporative emission control and misfire checks. A drive cycle is a prescribed sequence of start, warm-up, speeds and stops that lets the monitors run. The malfunction indicator lamp (MIL) is the dashboard lamp. When a fault is confirmed, the ECU stores the DTC and lights the MIL. Service 04 can clear the codes and turn the lamp off, but the fault remains if the cause is not repaired. Permanent codes in service 0A stay until the relevant self-test passes.

items: CAN runs at 500 kbit/s with 11-bit identifiers, or at 250 kbit/s with 29-bit identifiers, for OBD-II messages.
OBD-II is emissions-focused: generic services expose engine and emission data.
Manufacturer enhanced diagnostics go deeper into ABS, airbag, body and other modules.

figure.caption: A scan tool reaches the engine ECU through the J1962 connector and CAN bus. The ECU stores the fault code and freeze frame, and it drives the dashboard lamp.

spec.title: Path from scan tool to fault code
spec.aria: Block diagram: a scan tool plugs into the 16-pin connector, reaches the ECU over CAN, reads stored fault codes and freeze-frame data, and the ECU drives the malfunction lamp.

examples.question: A scan tool requests PID 0C, engine speed. The reply gives data bytes A = 0x1A and B = 0xF0. Find the engine speed in rpm.
steps: Divide by 4 because each count is 0.25 rpm: 6896 ÷ 4 = 1724 rpm.
examples.check:
a = 0x1A
b = 0xF0
raw = a * 256 + b
rpm = raw // 4
print(rpm)

traps: The P in P0301 means powertrain, not petrol. C is chassis, B is body, U is network.
P0301 is a generic misfire code for cylinder 1. A code such as P1xxx is manufacturer-specific and needs enhanced diagnostics beyond the standard services.
Pins 4 and 5 are ground, and pin 16 is battery positive. Do not treat pin 16 as a signal pin.
Freeze frame is stored data from the moment a fault was set, not live data. Use service 02, not service 01, to read it.
Clearing codes with service 04 turns off the MIL but does not repair the fault; permanent codes may remain until a self-test passes.

quiz.q: In the DTC P0301, what does the letter P mean?
quiz.a: P means powertrain. The other letters are C for chassis, B for body and U for network.

quiz.q: Which service reads stored diagnostic trouble codes?
quiz.a: Service 03 reads stored DTCs. Service 01 reads current data and service 02 reads the freeze frame.

quiz.q: Why does OBD-II define both ground pins and a battery pin on the J1962 connector?
quiz.a: The ground pins give the scan tool a common reference, and pin 16 supplies fused battery positive so the tool can power up before the car is started. The signal pins then carry bus messages.

quiz.q: PID 0C returns A = 0x0C and B = 0x80. Calculate the engine speed in rpm.
Decode the generic DTC P0301 into its letter, first digit, second digit and last two digits.
quiz.a: P means powertrain. The first digit 0 means a generic code. The second digit 3 means ignition system or misfire. The last two digits 01 mean cylinder 1.

quiz.q: A driver clears the codes with a scan tool. The MIL goes off, but it returns the next day. Explain what happened.
quiz.a: Service 04 cleared the stored codes and turned off the lamp, but the physical fault remained. When the ECU completed the relevant monitor and confirmed the fault again, it stored the DTC and lit the MIL. Permanent codes may also have stayed until a self-test passed.

quiz.q: Why can a generic OBD-II scan tool fail to read an ABS fault on some cars?
quiz.a: OBD-II generic services are emissions-focused and cover the engine and emission-related modules. ABS may sit on a different module and use manufacturer-specific services and codes. A tool needs enhanced diagnostics for that maker to reach it.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, OBD-II data feeds fleet telematics, insurance dongles and inspection apps through the same J1962 socket. Engineers build enhanced diagnostic layers on top of the generic services to reach body, braking and safety modules. Search next for J1979 service definitions, PID scaling tables, readiness monitor drive cycles and 29-bit CAN OBD-II. Newer work connects diagnostic data to over-the-air updates and remote fault prediction.
